hints: Notice the measured quantity is not $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ or $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ but the rise $100 - 40 = 60^{\circ}\text{C}$, which needs two separate thermometer readings.
Recall that for addition or subtraction the absolute uncertainties add, so the $\pm 0.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ from the start and the $\pm 0.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ from the end must be combined.
Divide the combined absolute uncertainty in $^{\circ}\text{C}$ by the $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ rise and multiply by $100\%$ to get percentage uncertainty.
walkthrough: Find the temperature change from the two readings: $\Delta T = 100^{\circ}\text{C} - 40^{\circ}\text{C} = 60^{\circ}\text{C}$.
State the uncertainty rule for a difference: absolute uncertainties add, so each $\pm 0.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ reading contributes.
Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the rise: $\Delta(\Delta T) = 0.5^{\circ}\text{C} + 0.5^{\circ}\text{C} = 1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Set up percentage uncertainty as absolute uncertainty divided by measured value: $(1.0/60) \times 100\%$.
Evaluate and check units cancel to leave percent: $(1.0/60) \times 100\% \approx 1.67\% \approx 1.7\%$.

options.A: This is too small and ignores both the $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ rise and the doubling of the $\pm 0.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ reading uncertainty.
options.B: This is $0.5/60 \times 100\%$, which counts the $\pm 0.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ uncertainty from only one of the two temperature readings.
options.C: This is about $0.5/40 \times 100\%$, which uses the starting $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ instead of the $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ temperature change.
options.D: Total absolute uncertainty is $0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$ in a $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ rise, giving $1.0/60 \times 100\% \approx 1.7\%$.
